intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.

widget.instructions: Drag point P along the line, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to read the velocity at any moment.

stem: A cyclist's velocity rises steadily from {{u}} m/s to {{v}} m/s over {{t}} s, as the velocity–time graph shows.
How far does the cyclist travel in those {{t}} seconds?

hints.text: On a velocity–time graph, what does the area under the line stand for?
Split the region under the line into a rectangle and a triangle.

area-uses-final-velocity.text: {{v}} m/s × {{t}} s assumes the cyclist moved at the final speed the whole time. The coral region is what you counted; the cyclist only covered the orange area under the line.

area-ignores-acceleration.text: {{u}} m/s × {{t}} s is only the rectangle under the starting speed. The cyclist sped up, so the coral triangle on top counts too.

area-misses-rectangle.text: That's only the triangle. The cyclist was already moving at the start, so the coral rectangle underneath counts as well.

slope-instead-of-area.text: That's the slope of the line (rise over run), which is the acceleration. Distance is the area under a velocity–time graph, not its slope.

dimension-mismatch.text: Distance is a length. Check your unit.

unit-conversion-error.text: Check your unit conversion. The graph uses metres and seconds.

generic.text: Distance on a velocity–time graph is the area under the line. Which shapes make up that area?

workedSolution.text: Displacement equals the area under the velocity–time graph from 0 to {{t}} s.
Rectangle under the starting speed: {{u}} m/s × {{t}} s = {{rect}} m.
Triangle for the gain in speed: ½ × ({{v}} − {{u}}) m/s × {{t}} s = {{tri}} m.

steps.text: For steady acceleration the average velocity is halfway between the start and end: ({{u}} + {{v}})/2 = {{(u+v)/2}} m/s.
Distance = average velocity × time = {{(u+v)/2}} × {{t}} = {{s}} m. The rectangle under the average-velocity line has the same area as the region under the graph.

area-uses-final-velocity.front: Velocity rises from u to v in time t. Why isn't the distance v × t?
area-uses-final-velocity.back: The body was slower earlier. Distance is the area under the v–t line: rectangle u·t plus triangle ½(v − u)t.

area-ignores-acceleration.front: Speeding up from u to v: is the distance u × t?
area-ignores-acceleration.back: No. That is only the rectangle. Add the triangle ½(v − u)t for the speed gained.

area-misses-rectangle.front: Which shapes make up the area under a rising v–t line that starts at u > 0?
area-misses-rectangle.back: A rectangle u·t under the starting speed plus a triangle ½(v − u)t on top.

slope-instead-of-area.front: On a v–t graph, what do the slope and the area tell you?
slope-instead-of-area.back: Slope = acceleration. Area under the line = displacement.

generic.front: How do you get distance from a velocity–time graph?
generic.back: Find the area under the line between the two times.
